business.what_it_does: A tool to collect text, image and video testimonials from customers and turn them into widgets, images, Walls of Love and case studies to share on websites, emails, ads and socials.
business.category: Testimonial collection and social proof software
business.business_model: Subscription SaaS, self-serve signup, with a permanent free tier and paid plans billed per month plus per-seat and per-project add-ons.

segments.name: A solo course-and-newsletter creator whose last launch converted worse than the one before, sitting on glowing DMs they have never once used on a sales page
segments.situation: They sell their own digital products — a course, a cohort, a paid newsletter — to an email list they built themselves, and they are the only voice on every page: their headline, their promise, their screenshots. Praise does arrive, but it arrives in the worst possible container: a DM after a cohort call, a reply to a broadcast, a kind line at the end of an offboarding email. Nothing is ever asked for formally, so nothing is ever structured, dated or attributed. When they do want proof for a launch, the workflow is a screenshot from a phone, a crop in Canva and a post, which is enough friction that it happens for the two or three favourite customers and no one else. Their site has a testimonials section that was filled in once, a year ago, with first names and no photos. They read creator Twitter, so they have heard the phrase 'social proof' a hundred times and feel vaguely behind on it; what they have not done is sit down and build a system for it, because proof feels like the thing you do after the product, and the product is never finished. This profile is reasoned from the supplied material, which names creators as the first of Senja's stated customer types and carries creator-side customer statements; the specifics of their week are inferred, not observed.

Design is a bottleneck for anything visual, so quotes go out as plain text or not at all. Asks for new testimonials happen in bursts after a launch and then stop, because nobody owns the follow-up. objections.objection: Will automated requests make me seem pushy?
Will offering an incentive make testimonials seem fake?
Can a student submit both video and written answers to the same question?

objections.objection: Where can I use collected student videos?

objections.objection: My students' results are mine to prove, but tying a testimonial to a reward or to unlocking content looks coercive — and a tool does not make people comfortable filming themselves.
I can do all of this for free with a Google Form, a spreadsheet and Canva. Paying monthly for testimonials is paying for a solved problem.
objections.answer: The strongest counter in the evidence is a customer who did exactly that: Alex Borto ran testimonials in Google Sheets and calls it 'a real mess' before switching, and Michael Heap's complaint is the assembly step rather than the collecting — logging in, making a graphic, copying it across, until 'most testimonials just became digital dust'. The comparison can also be made without a budget conversation, since the Free plan is $0 forever with no credit card [E146, E96]. The parts a DIY stack genuinely cannot do: unlimited ad-free video hosting [E222], automatic transcription of every video [E16], several submitted videos stitched into one multiclip [E7], and 20+ no-code widget templates [E157]. What the evidence does not have is any measurement of what the DIY stack costs in hours, so this must be argued with the customer quotes, not with a number.

objections.objection: $29 a month is more than I spend on anything that doesn't make money directly, and the free plan's 15-testimonial cap is exactly where it starts hurting.
objections.answer: Starter is $29/month, Pro $59/month, both cancel anytime [E162, E173]; yearly billing gives two months free and registered nonprofits get a discount [E189, E188]; Free is $0 forever, 15 testimonials, no card [E146, E96]. Leaving is genuinely cheap: on cancel or downgrade you drop to Free at the end of the billing period with a 10-day grace period, testimonials stay, and forms, widgets, links and embeds keep working [E184, E185]. Be honest about where it bites, because the reader will find it anyway: past 15 testimonials new ones are hidden until you upgrade, widgets and Walls of Love show Senja branding again on Free, and removing branding needs a paid plan [E183, E186, E45]. There is no money-back guarantee to lean on — only case-by-case refunds for billing errors, unused accounts and missed renewal notices, with a 1-2 business day reply and 5-10 business days to the original payment method [E195]. No student discount, and coupon-site codes do not work [E190].

objections.objection: My customers won't record a video of themselves. Asking feels like begging, and the ones who say yes will drop out halfway through the form.
objections.answer: Partly answerable. A Senja form is a personalised page where someone leaves a text or video testimonial in about 30 seconds, with no account and no software to install [E39, E40]; a form can be limited to text only or video only and questions can be text, video or rating, so the ask can be shrunk to a star rating [E52, E51]; up to three follow-ups go out automatically 1, 3 and 7 days later, and can be paused for one person [E27, E35]; a paid plan adds a recorded welcome video explaining why the testimonial matters [E2], and rewards exist [E209]. What the evidence does not fix, and copy should not pretend otherwise: every question you show is mandatory, there is no optional-question setting yet, and a customer cannot answer the same question in both video and text [E12, E5], so a longer form raises drop-off. Senja's own audio format was retired because end-user adoption was poor [E17]. The 'collect 3x more video testimonials' and 'twice as many' figures are unattributed with no baseline or method, so they cannot carry this objection [E77, E164, E207].

objections.objection: I've got maybe four testimonials. There's nothing here to manage yet — I'll look at a tool when I have a pile of them.
objections.answer: The starting pile is whatever already exists on the web. Senja imports existing testimonials from Google, X, LinkedIn, Product Hunt, G2 and more [E20], bulk-imports from CSV or XLSX [E23], and the Chrome extension grabs a testimonial from any page open in the browser [E21] — available on the free tier per the compare page [E90]. If they would rather not touch it, there is a free concierge migration that moves everything over [E182]. Collection itself is also not gated: text, image and video collection, the default form, and invites with tracking work on Free, Starter and Pro [E18, E19, E26]. The honest limit on this answer is the Free cap of 15 collected or imported testimonials [E96, E83].

objections.objection: We already run something for this — the widgets are embedded across the site and the review history sits in that tool. Ripping it out and re-embedding everywhere is a day I'm not getting back.
objections.answer: Free concierge migration moves everything over for you [E182]; imports cover 35 named sources including X, Facebook, Google, Capterra, Airbnb, Zillow and TrustPilot, plus CSV and existing mailing lists [E181, E23, E38]; widgets are paste-in embeds with no code, 20+ templates [E157, E138, E99]; case studies published elsewhere can be imported too [E74]. What nothing in the evidence addresses: pulling the incumbent's embeds off your pages, carrying over an aggregate star rating or review-platform standing, or any SEO continuity beyond Senja's own rich snippets [E106, E179]. Vendor comparison pages are Senja's claims about rivals, not verification, so they prove nothing here [E89, E92].

objections.objection: Social proof is not my bottleneck. My problem is traffic and the offer — a wall of testimonials won't move revenue.
objections.answer: This is the objection the evidence answers worst, and copy must not bluff it. The only revenue statement from a customer is Jay Clouse's, and it carries no figures: 'I've already seen a tangible impact on revenue and conversion by sharing more social proof' [E203]. Everything else is vendor assertion flagged as unmeasured — 'increase your conversion rates', 'growing faster with Senja' [E99, E75]. What can be offered honestly is measurement rather than a promise: widget analytics show views and clicks on widgets and Walls of Love [E160], testimonial analysis surfaces what customers actually say they value, in their words [E114, E139], and rich snippets put star ratings into search results [E179, E106]. No conversion-lift number exists in this evidence, so none may be implied.

provenance.quote: I’ve already seen a tangible impact on revenue and conversion by sharing more social proof.

objections.objection: This is a four-person remote company and I'd be handing them my customers' videos and the embeds on my homepage. If they fold or get acquired, my proof goes with them.
objections.answer: Only partly answerable. Every plan includes exports — text to CSV, video downloads, SD on Free and HD on Starter and Pro [E88, E156, E187] — and on downgrade the testimonials stay while links and embeds keep working [E185]. A project with its testimonials, forms and settings can be handed to another account entirely [E199]. One customer vouches for responsiveness and shipping: Nathan Falceso cites 'constant presence with their customers to address bugs and bring in new features' [E232]. Nothing in the evidence covers uptime, security, data processing terms, video-hosting durability or what happens to embedded widgets if the company changes hands, so this objection cannot be closed with what we currently know — the most we can do is name the export and transfer paths and stop there.

objections.objection: Their own pages don't agree on what I get. One page says 15 free testimonials, another says unlimited free collection; imports are 18 sites here, 20 there, 30+ somewhere else and 35 in the FAQ. If the pricing page can't be trusted, why would the product be?
objections.answer: Nothing in the supplied evidence resolves this — the conflict is inside Senja's own marketing. The pricing page caps the free tier at 15 collected or imported testimonials while a comparison page describes unlimited free video and text collection, and import coverage is stated four different ways on pages that sit beside each other. The only safe handling downstream is to quote the pricing page's figures and nothing else, never to repeat an import count in the same email as a free-tier claim, and to drop the superlatives ('most generous free tier of any social proof tool', 'the most generous out there', 'only on Senja'), which are flagged in the ledger as unsupported comparisons. This is a real finding: a product-aware reader who checks will catch us, so the copy should under-claim.

objections.objection: As an agency the per-client maths kills it: Starter gives me one project, Pro gives me five, and after that it's $10 a month per extra client plus $5 a seat. My small clients aren't worth that.
objections.answer: The numbers are at least transparent: Starter is 1 project and 2 seats with 3 forms; Pro is 5 projects and 5 seats with unlimited forms, extras at $10/month per project and $5/month per seat [E176, E177, E197, E198]. The lever that changes the maths is handover — support will transfer a project with its testimonials, forms and settings to the client's own account, links and embeds keep working, and the new owner takes over billing from there [E199]. Senja states plainly that it works for agencies inviting multiple clients [E196]. What is not in the evidence: any agency, reseller or volume tier, or any discount for project count. So a ten-client roster is Pro plus five project add-ons, and we should say so rather than imply a bulk rate exists.

objections.objection: I could build this myself. A collection form and a quote grid is an afternoon's work, and then I own it.
objections.answer: The form and the grid are the easy half. The parts that are not an afternoon: unlimited ad-free video hosting built in, positioned as a replacement for Wistia, YouTube and Vimeo [E222, E223]; automatic transcription of every video so it is searchable as text [E16]; multiclip stitching several submitted videos into one [E7]; 20+ widget templates and 23 named widget styles [E157, E220]; rich snippets for star ratings in search [E106]; and the entire collection side — invites with follow-ups at 1, 3 and 7 days, per-customer pause, and status tracking across sent, opened, clicked, collected, declined, undelivered and unsubscribed [E27, E35, E32, E33]. If the instinct is control rather than cost, Zapier, webhooks and the API are already there [E171, E172, E104], as is an MCP integration and a Slack bot [E218, E217].

objections.objection: Not now. I'll sort proof out after the launch, once there are customers worth quoting.
objections.answer: Starting costs nothing and needs no card, so 'not now' has no price attached [E146, E96], and a form can be customised and shared in about a minute [E150, E133]. Jamie Northrup's account is the useful one for a reader who expects a project: 'Took me less than 5 minutes to start collecting them, and adding them to my website was even quicker' [E213]. The argument for doing it before the launch rather than after is auto-collect, which fires the request at the moment a customer buys, finishes a course or gets tagged in a CRM, with reminders stopping as soon as they submit — but it needs Starter or Pro [E49, E46, E22], and Stripe can trigger invites from the Invites tab [E36]. One trap worth naming: follow-ups are not retroactive, so anyone invited before you switch them on gets no reminders [E29]. Nothing in the evidence quantifies the cost of waiting, so do not invent one.
